title: The teacher who is just run down
key_questions: how often are you passing water
key_question_reasons: Twelve kilos lost without trying, hidden behind 'a new diet', is the classic new type 1 story.
Polydipsia: four to five litres a day and still parched is osmotic, not a hot classroom.
Polyuria five or six times a night completes the triad she calls 'humiliating'.
Blurred vision that comes and goes is osmotic lens swelling from high glucose.
Vomiting and abdominal pain for two days are the ketoacidosis itself, and the reason she is drowsy tonight.
name: Rita
description: Year-nine physics teacher, three years into the job at a big comprehensive. Lives with her flatmate Priya two streets from school and runs on coffee and marking. Priya drove her in after finding her asleep on the bathroom floor this afternoon; Rita says she was resting.

presentation.duration: Two days of vomiting; several weeks of being 'run down'
presentation.triage_note: Brought by flatmate. Vomiting for two days, unable to keep fluids down, generalised abdominal pain, drowsy but rousable. Flatmate says she has 'not been herself for weeks' and is 'never off the toilet'. Looks dry. Breathing fast and deep.

past_medical: Nothing. I've never been in hospital in my life
medications: Ibuprofen for headaches, more than I should probably
allergies: Penicillin gave me a rash as a kid
social: I teach year nine physics. Three years now
I live with my flatmate, Priya, near the school
I joined a gym in January
family: Dad's fine. Grandad had something with his stomach late in life

opening_line: I only came because my flatmate wouldn't let it go. I'm just run down.
personality: Sharp, a little defensive. A teacher, used to being the one in charge of a room. Deflects with dry humour. Hates being fussed over and will minimise anything you ask about. Warms up if you are straight with her.
symptoms: I am thirsty constantly, no matter how much I drink
I am up five or six times a night to use the toilet
my clothes have gone loose over the last two months
my vision goes soft and blurry, then clears again
I was so tired I fell asleep at my desk at lunch
my stomach has been off for days and I can't keep anything down since yesterday
lie: I started a new diet in the spring. That's all the weight is.
truth: I've lost about twelve kilos without trying. I drink four or five litres a day and still wake up parched. I've been scared to say it out loud.
cracks_when: pressed on it a second time, or asked what her flatmate has noticed
red_herrings: joined a gym in January and blames the weight on that
term has been brutal and she assumes it is stress

canned.how much are you drinking: Constantly. There's a bottle on my desk and it is never enough.
canned.how often are you passing water: All night, if you must know. Five, six times. It's humiliating.
canned.is your vision blurry: It goes soft sometimes, then it comes back. I need new glasses, that's all.
canned.abdominal pain or vomiting: My stomach's been off for days. I can't keep anything down since yesterday. It's probably the bug going round school.
canned._greeting: Hi. Sorry, you're wasting a bed on me. I'm just run down.
canned._whats_wrong: I have no idea. You're the one in the white coat.
_deflect: I'm run down. Term has been brutal.
I joined a gym in January. That'll be it.
Can we be quick? I have marking to do.
Everyone's tired in November. This is not news.
My flatmate is a worrier. Don't take her word for anything.
canned._feeling: I am fine. I would be more fine at home marking books.

exam.general: Drowsy, GCS 14 (E3 V5 M6). Deep, sighing respirations at 28/min. A sweet, acetone smell on the breath. Thin; clothes visibly loose.
exam.hydration: Dry mucous membranes, reduced skin turgor, sunken eyes. Capillary refill 3 seconds. Clinically dehydrated.
exam.abdominal: Generalised mild tenderness without guarding or rebound. Bowel sounds present.
exam.cardiovascular: Tachycardic, 118 regular. BP 96/58 with a postural drop. Cool peripheries.
exam.neurological: GCS 14. No focal deficit. Reflexes normal.
exam.eyes: No retinopathy. Acuity 6/9 both eyes; she says it has been blurry on and off.

investigations.vbg: pH 7.08, pCO2 2.1 kPa, HCO3 6 mmol/L, base excess -22, lactate 2.1 mmol/L, glucose 31.4 mmol/L, K 5.6, Na 129.
investigations.abg: On room air: pH 7.09, pO2 13.1 kPa, pCO2 2.0 kPa, HCO3 6 mmol/L, lactate 2.1 mmol/L.
investigations.urine_dip: Glucose 4+, ketones 4+, protein trace. Blood, leucocytes and nitrites negative.
investigations.ue: Na 129 mmol/L, K 5.6 mmol/L, urea 12.4 mmol/L, creatinine 118 micromol/L, eGFR 52.
investigations.fbc: Hb 152 g/L, WCC 14.2 x10^9/L (neutrophils 11.1), platelets 380 x10^9/L.
investigations.lipase: Lipase 210 U/L (mildly raised; commonly seen with ketosis, not itself pancreatitis)
investigations.ecg: Sinus tachycardia 118/min. Peaked T waves in V2 to V4.

cxr.result: Clear lung fields. Normal cardiac silhouette.

harmful_treatments.nsaid: An NSAID in a dehydrated patient with acute kidney injury worsens renal function and adds nothing.
harmful_treatments.benzodiazepine_sedation: Her deep breathing is compensating for a profound acidosis. Sedation blunts that drive and can precipitate respiratory failure.

management_points: Recognise the triad: glucose above 11, ketones 3 or more, and acidosis (pH below 7.3 or bicarbonate below 15)
Fixed-rate IV insulin infusion at 0.1 units/kg/hour, started once fluids are running
IV 0.9% sodium chloride: the first litre over an hour, faster with a bolus if hypotensive
Potassium in the second and subsequent bags once K is below 5.5, with monitoring; peaked T waves now, but it will fall fast
Hourly glucose and ketones, a venous gas at 1, 2, 4 and 6 hours, and 10% glucose alongside once glucose is below 14
Find the precipitant: this is a new diagnosis of type 1; think infection and missed insulin in known patients
Diabetes specialist team on the day of admission; critical care if pH is below 7.0, GCS falls, or potassium is unsafe

teaching.summary: A new presentation of type 1 diabetes in a 31-year-old, weeks of osmotic symptoms hidden behind 'a new diet' and 'a brutal term', now in ketoacidosis with Kussmaul breathing and a pH of 7.08. She is not run down; she is hours from a critical care bed.
pearls: Weight loss without trying plus thirst plus nocturia is type 1 until proven otherwise, at any age.
A capillary ketone meter gives you the diagnosis at the bedside in one minute.
Fluids first, then fixed-rate insulin. Never bolus insulin; never hold it because glucose is falling: add glucose instead.
Potassium looks high on the first gas and crashes within hours of insulin. Plan the replacement before it happens.
Kussmaul breathing is a sign, not a symptom to sedate.

level_card: She teaches year nine and has not sat down in four hours.
She thinks she is wasting your time.
